extracted.intended_audience: scholars and educated readers interested in biblical geography, antiquarian history, and historical philology
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and arguing for the geographic location of the biblical Ophir using evidence from scriptural texts, classical historians, linguistic/onomastic traces, archaeology, natural history (fauna/flora), and maritime/navigation logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cargo-match with local produce
rubrics_metrics.description: That all the articles enumerated as forming the cargoes of the ships belonging to Solomon which visited Ophir were procurable in the country where Ophir was situated; therefore the produce lists in Scripture should match the natural and commercial products of the proposed location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the biblical catalogue (gold, silver, ivory, apes, peacocks, almug/precious woods, precious stones, spices, etc.) as a checklist: a plausible Ophir must supply these or their reasonable equivalents. The author applies this test to India, Ceylon, Sofala (east Africa), noting that all articles are found at Sofala (perhaps except peacocks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical and ancient historical testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts by ancient writers (e.g., Josephus, Herodotus, Diodorus, Pliny, Ptolemy) identifying Ophir or describing voyages/sources relevant to Ophir should be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh Josephus's statement equating Ophir with a Chersonesus Aurea in India and other classical references (e.g., Pliny's 'littus Hammœum') against each other. Consider the reliability and context of each source when using as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Septuagint and philological renderings
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic evidence such as the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew name (‎‏אוֺפִיר‏‎ → Σωφιρ, Σουφιρ, Σωφιρά) and other name-forms should be used to infer geographic associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare ancient translations and phonetic variants; the Septuagint forms are taken as the Egyptian name for India by some commentators, supporting an Indian identification. Collect variant forms from diverse sources and languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onomastic/toponymic continuity and name-variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace variants of the name Ophir across languages and historical sources (Uphaz, Paz, Paravim, Orphe, Appa, Efi, Ofor, Ophor, etc.) to identify likely geographic continuity or migration of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative forms across Biblical books, Greek/Roman writers, Arabic, and later geographers to argue for a region where the name (or close derivatives) survives. The author cites many variants and uses them to argue for Arabian associations (e.g., Ofor) or other localizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political/economic control of trade routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider which polities or emporia controlled the relevant trade routes (e.g., Tadmor/Palmyra, Phoenician colonies, Arabian emporia) because such control affects whether Solomon’s fleet would need to sail to a given region directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a power (e.g., Phoenician colonies in the Persian Gulf or Tadmor commanding caravan routes) already monopolised trade from India to Tyre/Jerusalem, a direct voyage by Solomon's fleet to the distant source might be unnecessary. Use this to argue for or against proposed locations (the author uses this to object to Persian Gulf and some Arabian theories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime plausibility: ships, navigation, and voyage duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the ships, seamanship, and navigational knowledge of the period could undertake the proposed voyage: considerations include ship type, need to put into harbours, pilots, compass absence, shores/reefs of Red Sea, and typical voyage durations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruct sailing seasons and timetable: the author models a three-year round trip from Ezion-geber to Sofala and back, invoking monsoon timings, refitting at emporia (Aden, Berbera), need for local pilots, and limits on night navigation. Use practical seamanship constraints to test candidate locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monsoon and wind-pattern compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposed sea-route must be consistent with known regional wind and monsoon patterns (e.g., NE monsoon Nov–Apr, SW return winds), which determine when voyages could depart, trade seasons, and return times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match proposed departure and return months to monsoon cycles and local seasonal weather; the author uses this to show a realistic timetable for a voyage to Sofala (e.g., leaving Ezion-geber in July, reaching Sofala with the NE monsoon timing, trading during six months, and returning with the SW monsoon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of species and botanical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Faunal and floral evidence (e.g., peacocks, parrots, ebony, almug/almug trees, myrrh, aloes, cinnamon, cassia) should correspond to the natural history of the candidate region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check species distributions: the author notes peacock/parrot identification is disputed (peacock is Indian but some translate as parrots or guinea-fowl) and points out ebony and almug trees and gold at Sofala. Differences in species distributions can disqualify or support a location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaeological remains and inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Material evidence such as ruins and inscriptions (e.g., Zimboë inscriptions, ruins at Fura/Afura) can provide direct support for identifying Ophir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek inscriptions that name peoples/places or ruins whose local traditions tie them to famous figures (Queen of Sheba, Solomon). The author cites João dos Sanctos' report of ruins and local tradition associating them with the Queen of Sheba or Solomon’s factory; inscriptions might definitively resolve location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local traditions and travel accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Eyewitness and local testimony (e.g., João dos Sanctos, Portuguese accounts, Moorish traditions) about mines, ruins, and trade practices can be used as supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accounts of contemporary inhabitants and resident witnesses regarding gold sources, ruins, and trading practices, while noting their limitations and potential for myth-making. The author uses such accounts to argue for Sofala.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative biblical textual analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare variant readings within biblical books (e.g., differences between 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles on 'Tharshish/Tarshish' and trip frequency) and interpret ambiguous Hebrew phrases (e.g., 'every three years' vs 'every third year') to refine logistical conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine textual differences and Hebrew idioms (counting broken years as whole, 'third year' meaning less than three full years) to infer realistic voyage durations and the identity of Tarshish, which affects whether Ophir lies east (Africa/India) or west (Tartessus/Spain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phoenician trade patterns and fleet practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand Phoenician commercial habits (e.g., using 'ships of Tharshish' for long-range merchantmen, tendency to preserve nautical records) when assessing whether such a voyage is likely or would have been recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider typical Phoenician routes, whether they carried out circumnavigations, and how they named ship-classes; the presence or absence of Phoenician records and consistency with their known trading network is an evidentiary factor (author questions a very early circumnavigation claim on these grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topographical/logistical fit with inland waterways and river access
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed Ophir location requires fleets to use river systems (e.g., driving trade up Tigris/Euphrates), assess navigability and whether such routes would have been used or necessary given existing trade infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calmet's Armenian/Persian Gulf theory depends on river navigation to inland sources; the author objects that Tadmor and the Phoenician control of Persian Gulf trade would render such a fleet unnecessary. Verify practical river access and comparative advantage over overland/caravan routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and convergence of multiple lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer hypotheses supported by several independent evidence types (textual, linguistic, archaeological, natural history, maritime logistics, classical testimony) rather than isolated indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author assesses competing theories (India, Persian Gulf, South Arabia, Sofala) by testing each against multiple criteria (products, winds, political control, toponymy, classical accounts) and favors the location with the best overall fit (here, Sofala) where most lines converge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of source reliability and skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise critical judgement about the credibility of sources (e.g., Herodotus’s skepticism about Phoenician claims, Josephus’s identifications, later travel narratives), not accepting ancient claims at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal consistency, plausibility, and corroboration between independent sources to weigh reliability. The author cites Herodotus's doubts about Phoenician reports as a cautionary example and prefers explanations consistent with known practices and records.
